design_detail: Two crossover laboratory studies in healthy fasting adult volunteers, reported together. In the first study, ketamine hydrochloride was given by intravenous injection (0.25 or 0.125 mg of base per kg of body weight) on separate occasions to five volunteers, with an injection of normal saline on a third occasion. In the second study, six volunteers received ketamine 0.5 mg/kg by intramuscular injection into the triceps of the dominant arm and 0.5 mg/kg as an oral solution in 50 mL of orange juice, on separate occasions, with normal saline as the comparison; on every occasion the person drank 50 mL of orange juice with or without ketamine and at the same time received an intramuscular injection of ketamine or saline, so that the route under test was masked. The order of administration was randomized, and the participant and the person recording pain scores were unaware of which solution had been given. Venous blood was taken over 7 hours; plasma ketamine and norketamine were measured as heptafluorobutyryl derivatives by gas chromatography with electron-capture detection; concentration-time data were fitted to a two-compartment open model by nonlinear regression, and bioavailability was computed from the ratio of dose-adjusted areas to each person's own intravenous curve. Pain threshold was measured in parallel with a modified ischaemic exercise test.
can_establish: The plasma kinetics of ketamine and its metabolite norketamine after intravenous, intramuscular and oral administration of analgesic amounts in healthy volunteers, the systemic availability of the intramuscular and oral routes relative to an intravenous reference, and the association between plasma ketamine concentration and pain threshold in an experimental ischaemic pain model within the same people.
cannot_establish: Whether ketamine relieves clinical pain in patients (no patient took part and no clinical pain was studied); the duration, size or variability of any analgesic effect with useful precision (four to six people per comparison, no confidence intervals); anything about anaesthetic amounts, repeated administration, women (sex is not reported), or people with ketamine experience; and any harm, since none was measured.

sample.recruitment: Not stated beyond 'healthy, fasting adult volunteers'; no recruitment source, screening, consent or ethics statement appears anywhere in the paper (p. 539).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond being healthy and fasting. No medical screening, medication history, drug or alcohol history, or exclusion criteria are reported (p. 539).
sample.demographics: First study: age 33.8 years (SE 1.4), weight 74.8 kg (SE 2.1), n = 5. Second study: age 31.8 years (SE 2.0), weight 70.7 kg (SE 4.4), n = 6. Sex is not reported for either study, and no individual characteristics are given (p. 539).
sample.attrition: Not reported. Table I prints intramuscular and oral bioavailability for four of the six people in the second study and gives no reason for the two gaps (p. 540).
sample.selection_effects: Eleven participants in two small volunteer samples of unstated origin, whose sex, health screening and prior drug experience are all unreported, and whose total is 11 only if the two studies had no participants in common, which the paper does not say. Nothing links this sample to patients in pain or to people who use ketamine outside medicine.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered and measured in the laboratory. Plasma was analysed in duplicate or triplicate for ketamine and norketamine as their heptafluorobutyryl derivatives by gas chromatography with electron-capture detection, with the method cited to three earlier papers; no limit of quantification, calibration range, precision or accuracy is printed. Dehydronorketamine consistently gave two chromatographic peaks, as an earlier group had found (pp. 539-540).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. First study: single intravenous injections of ketamine hydrochloride at 0.25 and 0.125 mg of base per kg on separate occasions, and normal saline on a third occasion. Second study: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg as a single intramuscular injection into the triceps of the dominant arm, and 0.5 mg/kg as an oral solution in 50 mL of orange juice, on separate occasions, with normal saline as the comparison; each session combined a drink and an injection. Blood (8 mL) was taken before dosing and at 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 and 45 minutes and at 1, 2, 4 and 7 hours (p. 539).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. No other drug, alcohol, tobacco or caffeine use is reported, and no screening for it is described; participants were fasting (p. 539).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants were fasting. The interval between occasions is not stated in either study, so no washout can be checked (p. 539).

comparison.controls: Within-person only: normal saline on a separate occasion in both studies, and each person's own intravenous concentration-time curve as the reference for bioavailability. There is no separate control group and no patient group.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with randomized order of administration; the method of randomization, the sequences used, and any test for a period or carryover effect are not reported (p. 539).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic questions. For the pain measures the only baseline is the 30-minute control period within each session, so any change over weeks cannot be separated from the condition.

outcomes.instruments: Pharmacokinetics: a two-compartment open model fitted by nonlinear regression with a simplex algorithm, data weighted as recommended by Ottaway, goodness of fit judged by a run test, a number test on the signs of the residuals and a serial-correlation statistic; absorption rate constants also estimated by the method of Loo and Riegelman; bioavailability (Farea) as the ratio of the trapezoidal area, corrected for the area beyond the last data point and adjusted for dose, after the intramuscular or oral dose to that after the intravenous dose in the same person; two further estimates of the first-pass fraction, one from clearance with hepatic blood flow taken as 1.53 L/min (Eq. 1) and one from the oral area (Eq. 2). Analgesia: a modification of the ischaemic exercise test of Harrison and Bigelow, scored both as a verbal pain score after 75-105 seconds of exercise ('none', 'mild', 'moderate', 'severe') and as the time to intolerable pain, during a 30-minute control period and at fixed times to 60 minutes in the first study and to 120 minutes in the second (p. 539).
outcomes.validity_norms: The ischaemic exercise test is an experimental pain model with no norms; its stability within this sample is shown by the control period, in which severe pain appeared after 75-105 seconds of exercise and was reproducible in each person on each occasion, with intolerable pain a further 7 seconds later (range 1-13 s) (p. 541). The chromatographic assay is cited to earlier papers and no validation data are reproduced.
outcomes.operationalization: A raised pain threshold is defined relative to the same person's control period on the same day: a pain score of 'none' or 'mild' at 75-105 seconds of ischaemic exercise, or a significant prolongation of the time to intolerable pain, or both (pp. 539, 541). In the Discussion a stricter criterion is used for the concentration threshold: a score of 'none' or 'mild' or an increase of at least 20 seconds in the time to intolerable pain (p. 541). Nothing is operationalized as harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Student's t test is the only test named, with no alpha stated (p. 540). It is applied across eight tabulated pharmacokinetic parameters by route, five absorption and bioavailability estimates, the comparison of plasma concentrations between the two pain-score groups, the pain measures at each of eight or nine time points after each route, and two correlations. No adjustment of any kind is reported and no confidence interval appears in the paper.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The participant and the person recording the pain scores were unaware of the nature of the administered solution, and the combined drink-and-injection design of the second study masked the oral and intramuscular conditions against each other (p. 539). Blinding integrity was not tested, and nothing is said about blinding of the assay or of the curve fitting.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard errors; no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes anywhere. Intravenous: terminal half-life 186 min (SE 10 in the Results text, SE 8 in Table II); dose-corrected AUC 27.5 (SE 1.2); total body clearance 19.1 mL/min/kg (SE 1.1) (pp. 540-541). Intramuscular 0.5 mg/kg: peak 243 ng/mL (SE 49) at 22 min (SE 4); half-life 155 min (SE 12); AUC 23.6 (SE 2.2); clearance 23.2 mL/min/kg (SE 2.7); bioavailability 0.930 (SE 0.026). Oral 0.5 mg/kg: peak 44 ng/mL (SE 10) at 30 min (SE 5); half-life 174 min (SE 50); AUC 4.8 (SE 0.8); bioavailability 0.166 (SE 0.028) by area and 0.195 (SE 0.028) by Eq. 2. Norketamine peaks 40 (SE 6), 92 (SE 10) and 200 ng/mL (SE 44) after the intravenous, intramuscular and oral conditions, with areas 35.4 (SE 3.8), 31.3 (SE 3.8) and 36.7 (SE 3.9), described as not significantly different (Table II, p. 541). Editors' calculation from the individual values in Table I: the intramuscular and oral area-based bioavailabilities are means of four people each (0.965, 0.923, 0.972, 0.859 and 0.145, 0.163, 0.112, 0.245), while the Eq. 2 estimate is a mean of six (0.160, 0.190, 0.155, 0.115, 0.309, 0.239); each printed standard error reproduces exactly on those sample sizes. Pain: plasma concentrations accompanying a 'none' or 'mild' score, 186 ng/mL (SE 23), against 101 ng/mL (SE 8) for 'moderate' or 'severe'; correlation between plasma ketamine concentration and the increase in time to intolerable pain r = 0.712, p < 0.001; no significant correlation for norketamine (pp. 540-541).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted within-person comparisons of means.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned, and the paper carries no ethics-approval or consent statement.
analysis.selective_reporting: Apparent distribution volumes of the central compartment, at steady state and in the terminal phase are defined in the methods but no values are printed. Table I gives absorption rate constants by the Loo-Riegelman method and bioavailability by area for only four of the six people in the second study, with no explanation, and prints no mean or standard error for either absorption rate constant. Several analgesia results are attributed to the two companion papers rather than reported here, including the duration of the intravenous effect and the significant prolongations at 15 and 30 minutes after the intramuscular dose. The pain data appear as two figures of individual observations and as significance statements, with no table.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With four to six people per comparison the estimates are imprecise: the oral half-life is 174 min with a standard error of 50 min, the individual oral estimates from Eq. 2 range from 0.115 to 0.309, and the intramuscular peak concentrations range from 100 to 425 ng/mL. Statements that parameters 'did not differ significantly' between routes or doses rest on these samples and are not evidence of equivalence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In healthy volunteers given analgesic amounts, plasma ketamine fell biexponentially after intravenous injection with a terminal half-life of about three hours; after intramuscular injection absorption was rapid and systemic availability was high (0.930, from four people), with a half-life no different from intravenous; after an oral solution only about a sixth of the dose reached the circulation (0.166, from four people) while norketamine concentrations were higher than after the other routes, which the authors read as extensive first-pass metabolism. In the ischaemic pain model, pain threshold rose for up to an hour after the intramuscular dose, when ketamine concentrations were 85-330 ng/mL, and barely at all after the oral solution, when they were 17-65 ng/mL.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that only 17% of an oral dose 'was absorbed because of extensive first-pass metabolism', which is the opposite of the paper's own argument: the Discussion assumes absorption from the gut lumen was complete and attributes the low concentrations to metabolism after absorption (pp. 539, 541). The abstract's headline bioavailability of 93% is a mean of four people, a sample size visible only in Table I. The abstract states a general threshold (pain threshold elevation at plasma concentrations above 160 ng/mL) without the Discussion's qualifying criterion or the fact that the figure behind it pools several observations per person. The Discussion closes by saying the data make it possible to design dosage regimens and may increase ketamine's usefulness as an analgesic, which goes beyond an experimental ischaemic pain model in a handful of healthy volunteers with no clinical pain outcome.

timeline.event: Companion study of intravenous ketamine kinetics and analgesia in healthy volunteers by two of the same authors (Clements & Nimmo, Br J Anaesth 53:27), cited here for the duration of the intravenous effect and for the comparison with anaesthetic amounts
Companion study of intramuscular and oral ketamine by the same three authors (Grant, Nimmo & Clements, Br J Anaesth 53:805), cited here for the pain-score results after intramuscular injection

Stereoselective kinetics in surgical patients (Geisslinger et al.) reported differences between the ketamine enantiomers that this racemate study could not see, since its assay was not stereoselective
Oral bioavailability of about 18% in three healthy Japanese men, close to the 17% found here, with higher availability by sublingual, rectal and nasal routes
Clinical pharmacokinetics review tabulates this study's values by route and carries forward intramuscular bioavailability of about 93% and oral bioavailability of 17-24%

replication.where_it_stands: The intramuscular figure of about 93% and the oral figure of about 17% are still the numbers carried in reviews more than thirty years later, and both come from this one report, each from four people with an intravenous reference. Neither has been independently re-measured in adults in the sources read here. The oral figure agrees with the later three-person Japanese study; the intramuscular figure has no independent check in those sources.

funding.funder: The Scottish Hospital Endowments Research Trust, thanked for financial support (Acknowledgments, p. 542).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears; the journal did not require one in 1982.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Pharmacy, Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, and departments of anaesthesia at the Western Infirmary, Glasgow, and Ninewells Hospital, Dundee. The preparation used is named as a commercial product of a pharmaceutical company in a footnote (p. 539), without saying whether the company supplied it or had any role. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A crossover study with every participant receiving an intravenous reference dose, in a sample large enough for interval estimates, in both sexes, with an enantiomer-specific assay of stated sensitivity and precision, half-lives reported for every route, and a pre-specified mixed-effects analysis of the concentration-effect relation that treats repeated measurements as nested within person rather than as independent observations.

domains.note: The order of administration is said to have been randomized in both studies, but no method of sequence generation, no allocation concealment and no sequences are described, and no period effect is reported or modelled.

The interval between occasions is not stated in either study. A blank sample was taken before each dose but its values are never reported, so carryover cannot be ruled out from the paper, although a terminal half-life of about three hours makes it unlikely if the occasions were days apart.

A double-dummy drink-plus-injection design masked the two extravascular routes, and the participant and the pain-score recorder were unaware of the solution given; but blinding integrity was not tested and ketamine at these amounts produces noticeable effects, so the masking of active against saline cannot be assumed.

Bioavailability by area is printed for four of six people after each extravascular route, and Loo-Riegelman absorption constants for four of six, with no explanation; the two people without them have the highest and one of the lowest nonlinear-regression absorption constants. The intravenous reference that these ratios require is described in a different study of five people, and which participants provided it is never stated.

The chromatographic assay is an objective measure but is unvalidated in this report: no limit of quantification, precision or accuracy is printed, and the oral terminal half-life is estimated from concentrations of 17-65 ng/mL. The pain outcomes are participant-reported in an experimental model, collected in a session the participant knew included an injection and a drink.

No protocol or pre-specified outcome; distribution volumes defined but not reported; several analgesia results attributed to the companion papers; and the concentration threshold of 160 ng/mL rests on a criterion that appears only in the Discussion, applied after the data were seen.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Within each person the design is sound for the pharmacokinetic questions: a randomized-order crossover with a double-dummy for the two extravascular routes and an intravenous reference for bioavailability. The overall judgment is set by the missing data, since the two headline figures (93% and 17%) are means of four people each, and by the fact that the intravenous reference needed for those ratios is described in a separate five-person study without saying who contributed it. The source can be cited for the plasma kinetics of ketamine and norketamine by the intravenous, intramuscular and oral routes at analgesic amounts in healthy volunteers, for the systemic availability of those routes with their sample sizes attached, and for the association between plasma concentration and experimental pain threshold within these people; it cannot be cited for the analgesic effect of ketamine in patients, for any threshold concentration as a general fact, for anaesthetic amounts or repeated use, or for anything about harm.

key_findings.finding: After intravenous injection, plasma ketamine concentrations were fitted by a two-compartment open model with a mean terminal half-life of 186 minutes; the Results give a standard error of 10 minutes and Table II gives 8 minutes for the same figure.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetics, 1st paragraph (p. 540); Table II, row 'Half-life (t1/2beta)', intravenous column (p. 541)
key_findings.note: The two standard errors for the same mean differ; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Bioavailability after intramuscular injection of 0.5 mg/kg was 0.930 (SE 0.026), the mean of four individual values (0.965, 0.923, 0.972 and 0.859); the other two people in the study have no value in that column.
key_findings.locator: Table I, column 'Farea' under 'Intramuscular Injection'; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the printed mean and standard error reproduce exactly on those four values, confirming n = 4 for the abstract's figure of 93%.

key_findings.finding: After the oral solution of 0.5 mg/kg, 16.6% of the dose reached the systemic circulation (Farea 0.166, SE 0.028, from four people: 0.145, 0.163, 0.112 and 0.245); the estimate from the oral area by Eq. 2 was 0.195 (SE 0.028) across all six people (0.160, 0.190, 0.155, 0.115, 0.309 and 0.239), and the estimate from intravenous clearance by Eq. 1, available for four people, agreed well with the observed values in only two of them.
key_findings.locator: Table I, oral-solution columns (p. 540); Results > Pharmacokinetics, 3rd paragraph (p. 540); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 541)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of the sample sizes from the printed means and standard errors: four people for the area-based figure and six for the Eq. 2 figure.

key_findings.finding: Tabulated parameters by route (mean with SE): peak concentration 243 ng/mL (49) at 22 min (4) after intramuscular and 44 ng/mL (10) at 30 min (5) after oral administration; terminal half-life 186 min (8) intravenous, 155 min (12) intramuscular and 174 min (50) oral; dose-corrected area 27.5 (1.2), 23.6 (2.2) and 4.8 (0.8); total body clearance 19.1 mL/min/kg (1.1) intravenous and 23.2 (2.7) intramuscular.
key_findings.note: The area units printed in Table II ('min ng/ml') are too small by about a factor of a thousand; see reporting issues. The table's footnote states N = 6 for all three columns, although the intravenous study is described in five people. Table II prints no peak concentration and no time to peak for the intravenous condition, so the only comparison of peak heights inside this paper is intramuscular against oral.

key_findings.finding: Absorption after intramuscular injection was rapid: apparent absorption half-times of 2-17 minutes, a lag before ketamine appeared in plasma of under 4 minutes, and peak concentrations between 100 and 425 ng/mL at 5-30 minutes. After the oral solution the lag was 4-13 minutes (mean 8.0) and the mean apparent peak was 44 ng/mL (range 15-80).

Norketamine was measurable after every route. Peak concentrations were 40 ng/mL (SE 6) after intravenous 0.25 mg/kg, 92 (10) after intramuscular and 200 (44) after oral administration, at 63, 78 and 60 minutes; the dose-corrected areas (35.4, 31.3 and 36.7) were similar and none differed significantly from the intravenous value, which the authors take as evidence that the low oral ketamine concentrations are due to first-pass metabolism rather than incomplete absorption.
key_findings.locator: Table II, norketamine block; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 4th paragraph (p. 540, continuing on p. 541); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 541)

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations accompanying a pain score of 'none' or 'mild' after 75-105 seconds of ischaemic exercise were significantly higher, 186 ng/mL (SE 23), than those accompanying 'moderate' or 'severe' scores, 101 ng/mL (SE 8), after intramuscular injection in six people.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 plots individual observations rather than people: roughly 10 points in panel (a) and about 18 in panel (b), counted from the rendered figure, from six participants, so the comparison treats several measurements per person as independent.

key_findings.finding: In the hour after intramuscular injection, plasma ketamine concentration was correlated with the increase in time to intolerable pain (r = 0.712, p < 0.001); no significant correlation was found for norketamine.
key_findings.note: Figure 2 plots about two dozen observations (counted from the rendered figure) from six people; degrees of freedom are not printed, and repeated measurements within a person are treated as independent. The correlation and p value are printed inside Figure 2 and were read from the figure rendered at 300 dpi; the machine-read text of this scanned page loses both decimal points, giving 'r = 0 712' and 'p < 0 001'.

key_findings.finding: Pain threshold was raised in every participant for up to one hour after intramuscular injection, with corresponding plasma ketamine concentrations of 85-330 ng/mL; in the Discussion the authors state that elevation occurred consistently above 160 ng/mL but not below 80 ng/mL, using the criterion of a 'none' or 'mild' score or an increase of at least 20 seconds in the time to intolerable pain.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pain Measurements, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: After the oral solution, pain thresholds were not markedly raised and participants reported moderate or severe pain; the mean increase in exercise time before intolerable pain was significant only at 30 minutes, when it was 9 seconds (0.05 > p > 0.025). Plasma ketamine was 17-65 ng/mL and norketamine was higher, 80-390 ng/mL, with no significant correlation between either and the increase in time to intolerable pain.

The duration of the pain-threshold elevation after intravenous injection (under 10 minutes after 0.25 mg/kg and under 5 minutes after 0.125 mg/kg) and the significant prolongations of exercise time at 15 and 30 minutes after intramuscular injection (24 and 21 seconds) are reported here with citations to the authors' two 1981 companion papers rather than as results of this study.
key_findings.note: A claim citing this paper for the time course of ketamine analgesia would be citing a secondary report of those companion studies.

key_findings.finding: The fitted intravenous curves are printed as biexponential equations: 82 exp(-0.044t) + 22 exp(-0.0039t) after 0.125 mg/kg and 108 exp(-0.039t) + 40 exp(-0.0038t) after 0.25 mg/kg, with concentration in ng/mL and time in minutes; no significant differences in the rate constants, apparent distribution volumes or clearance were found between the two amounts.

Clearance after intravenous injection (19.1 mL/min/kg) and after intramuscular injection (23.2) did not differ significantly, nor did the terminal half-lives (186 and 155 minutes), which the authors take as showing that the fall in plasma concentration after intramuscular injection represents elimination rather than continuing absorption.
key_findings.note: The non-difference is stated for the intramuscular condition only; no comparison of any kind is printed for the oral half-life of 174 min (SE 50), whose standard error is about a third of its mean.

key_findings.finding: The authors show that the length of the sampling period determines the half-life: analysing only the first 2 to 2.5 hours of their own intravenous data gives an apparent half-life of 105 minutes, against the 186 minutes obtained from sampling to 7 hours. They give this as the reason their figure is much longer than the 79 minutes reported at the end of an intravenous infusion elsewhere.
key_findings.note: This is the paper's own caution for comparing its half-life with studies that sample for a shorter period.

reporting_issues.issue: The intravenous terminal half-life is printed as 186 minutes with a standard error of 10 in the Results (twice, on p. 540) and as 186 with 8 in Table II (p. 541).
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot tell which dispersion belongs to the paper's most-cited figure; either should be quoted with the page it comes from.

reporting_issues.issue: Table II's footnote states N = 6 for all three columns, but the Experimental section describes the intravenous study in five volunteers and the intramuscular and oral study in six.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample size behind the intravenous parameters, including the 186-minute half-life and the clearance of 19.1 mL/min/kg, is ambiguous; the later review that tabulates these values records the intravenous row as n = 5.

reporting_issues.issue: Bioavailability is defined as the ratio of each person's extravascular area to their own intravenous area, yet the intravenous doses are described in the first study (five volunteers) and the intramuscular and oral doses in the second (six volunteers), and the paper never says which participants provided the intravenous reference or whether the two studies shared participants. Table I prints the ratio for four of the six.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the headline figures of 93% and 17% cannot be traced; claims should carry the sample size (four people) and this uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The area units in Table II are printed as 'min ng/ml' with values of 27.5, 23.6 and 4.8, which are about a thousand times too small for the stated concentrations and half-lives. Editors' calculation from the paper's own numbers: dose divided by clearance for the dose-corrected 0.5 mg/kg gives 0.5 mg/kg divided by 19.1 mL/min/kg, about 26 micrograms*min/mL, against the printed 27.5.
reporting_issues.consequence: The tabulated areas are internally consistent with one another and with clearance, but the printed unit is wrong by about three orders of magnitude; the values should never be quoted with the printed unit.

reporting_issues.issue: Eq. 1 is introduced as the fraction of the dose lost by first-pass metabolism, but it is written as one minus clearance divided by hepatic blood flow, which is the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism, and Table I and the Results use it as a bioavailability to be compared with the observed area ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's description of the equation contradicts its form and its use; a reader taking the text at face value would interpret the Eq. 1 column of Table I as the opposite of what it is.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that only 17% of an oral dose was absorbed because of extensive first-pass metabolism, and the Results say the same, calling absorption incomplete with only 16.6% of the dose reaching the systemic circulation, while the Discussion argues that absorption from the gut lumen was complete and that the loss happened after absorption, in the liver; the Eq. 2 calculation is explicitly made on the assumption of complete absorption.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract and the Results state as absorption what the paper attributes to metabolism; a claim about ketamine's oral absorption should follow the Discussion, and should not describe the absorption wording as the abstract's alone.

reporting_issues.issue: Figures 1 and 2 plot individual observations, not individual people: roughly 10 and about 18 points in the two panels of Figure 1, and about two dozen in Figure 2 (all counted from the rendered figures), from six participants. The t test comparing the two pain-score groups and the correlation of r = 0.712 treat these repeated measurements as independent, and no degrees of freedom are printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both p values are overstated relative to a six-person sample; the concentration threshold of 160 ng/mL derived from Figure 1 should be reported as an observation-level pattern in six people, not as an established threshold.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that absorption constants by the Loo-Riegelman method agreed with those from nonlinear regression except in one person in whom absorption was very rapid, but Table I omits the Loo-Riegelman constant for two people, whose nonlinear-regression constants are the highest (0.412) and among the lowest (0.069) in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The agreement between methods is asserted on four of six people, and the person with the fastest absorption is the one with no second estimate to compare.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites reference 14 for pharmacokinetics after anaesthetic amounts (2.5 mg/kg) in patients and for the terminal half-life of 151 minutes, but the Introduction attributes the 2.5 mg/kg study in five patients, with a half-life of 2.52 hours (151 minutes), to reference 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison between analgesic and anaesthetic amounts is attributed to two different sources in the same paper; anyone following the citation would reach the wrong study.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion explains the absence of an oral effect by saying concentrations did not exceed 80 ng/mL, while the Results give the oral range as 17-65 ng/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, and not a contradiction, but the two statements of the same range differ and only the Results value should be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: Apparent distribution volumes of the central compartment, at steady state and in the terminal phase are defined in the Pharmacokinetic Analysis section but no values are given anywhere in the paper, and the paper carries no statement of ethical approval or informed consent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The volume of distribution often attributed to this study cannot be taken from it; and the conduct of the study cannot be checked against any ethics statement.

The PDF is a scan with machine-read text, so every number was checked against the pages rendered at 150 dpi, with Table II and both figures re-rendered at 300 dpi. The reference record (J Pharm Sci 71(5):539-542, 1982) matches the printed first page. No supplementary material exists.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract says that only 17% of an oral dose was absorbed because of extensive first-pass metabolism, while the Discussion argues that absorption from the gut lumen was complete and that the loss happened after absorption, in the liver; the Eq. 2 calculation is explicitly made on the assumption of complete absorption.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 224, corrected: the absorption wording is not confined to the abstract; the Results on p. 540 also call absorption incomplete, with only 16.6% reaching the systemic circulation.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading pp. 539-541 on pages rendered at 150 dpi: the Results do say absorption was incomplete. Issue and consequence rewritten so that the contradiction runs between the abstract and the Results on one side and the Discussion on the other; page range widened to pp. 539-541.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 224, missed: the paper's own demonstration that sampling length determines the half-life (105 minutes from 2 to 2.5 hours of data against the 186 minutes reported).
disagreements.resolution: Added as a key finding after checking the Discussion's 1st paragraph on p. 541 rendered at 150 dpi. It is the paper's own caution and bears directly on comparing this half-life with the 2003 study, whose sampling ran to 8 hours.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 224, confirmed with an addition: the paper states the non-difference for the intramuscular route only and prints no test for the oral half-life.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: the Results (p. 540) test only the intramuscular half-life against the intravenous one, and no comparison for the oral half-life appears anywhere. Note added; the claim cl_ket_halflife_norketamine was corrected to match.

disagreements.first_pass: The area units printed in Table II ('min ng/ml') are too small by about a factor of a thousand; see reporting issues. The table's footnote states N = 6 for all three columns, although the intravenous study is described in five people.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 224, missed: Table II prints no time to peak and no peak concentration for the intravenous condition.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the rendered p. 541 (both cells are dashes) and added to the note, because it limits what peak comparisons this paper supports.
